title: Air your room every morning
excerpt: Ten minutes of fresh air before you head out keeps your room dry, fresh and free of mould.
steps: Once you’re dressed and ready for the day, open your bedroom window wide.
Leave it open for 10 to 15 minutes while you finish getting ready.
Close it before you leave.
If you can, do the same in the evening.
why: We breathe out a lot of moisture overnight. Letting it out each morning stops condensation and mould, and fresh air every day is good for your health too.

title: Last to shower? Let the steam out
excerpt: If you’re the last to shower, a wide-open window or 20 to 30 minutes of fan stops peeling paint and ceiling mould.
steps: Switch the extractor fan on before you shower.
If you’re the last to shower, open the window wide afterwards, or leave the fan running for 20 to 30 minutes.
Close the bathroom door behind you so the steam goes outside, not into the rest of the house.
Wipe the shower screen and tiles with a squeegee or towel.
why: Steam that stays in the bathroom settles on the ceiling and walls. That’s what makes paint peel and black mould grow.

title: Wipe your windows every morning
excerpt: Thirty seconds with a squeegee each morning stops black mould growing round your windows.
steps: Each morning, wipe the water off the glass with a squeegee or cloth.
Wring the cloth out into the sink, not onto the sill.
Wipe the window sill and frame dry too.
Open the window for a few minutes to finish drying it.
why: Water left on windows soaks into the sill and seals, and that’s where black mould starts.

title: Cooking? Lids on, fan on
excerpt: Lids on pans, the cooker fan on and the kitchen door closed: the easiest way to stop kitchen damp.
steps: Put lids on pans while you cook.
Turn the cooker hood fan on.
Keep the kitchen door closed while you cook.
Open a window if you can, and don’t leave the kettle boiling.
why: Cooking is one of the biggest sources of moisture in a home. Keeping the steam in the kitchen, and getting it outside, stops damp spreading.

title: Don’t dry clothes on the radiator
excerpt: A load of washing holds litres of water. Here’s where to dry it so it doesn’t end up on your walls.
steps: Dry washing outside whenever you can.
If it’s raining, put an airer in the bathroom with the door shut and the window open or the fan on.
Never dry clothes on radiators.
Ask yourself: where will all the water from the clothes go?
why: Clothes drying indoors put water straight into the air, and on radiators they also stop the room warming up.

title: Keep furniture off the walls
excerpt: Leave a hand’s width between furniture and walls so air can move and mould can’t hide.
steps: Leave a gap of about 23cm (9 inches) between beds, sofas and wardrobes and the walls, especially outside walls.
Don’t overfill wardrobes and cupboards.
Keep a little space between bedding and the wall.
why: Outside walls are colder. Where furniture blocks the air, condensation forms behind it and mould grows unseen.

title: Keep your trickle vents open
excerpt: That little slot at the top of your window lets your room breathe without a draught. Keep it open.
steps: Find the trickle vent along the top of the window frame.
Slide it open and leave it open all year.
Never cover vents, air bricks or chimneys.
why: Trickle vents let moist air out slowly all day and night, without making the room cold.

title: Running a bath? Cold tap first
excerpt: Run the cold tap first when you fill a bath and you’ll make a fraction of the steam.
steps: Put a few centimetres of cold water in the bath first.
Then top it up with hot.
Keep the fan on and the door shut while you bathe.
why: Hot water hitting an empty bath throws up clouds of steam. Cold water first keeps most of it in the water.

title: Clear the shower plughole every week
excerpt: A weekly 30-second clear-out keeps your shower draining and saves calling a plumber.
steps: Once a week, lift the plughole cover.
Pull out any hair with a tissue and put it in the bin.
Fit a hair catcher over the plughole; they cost a few pounds.
Don’t pour chemical drain cleaners down; report a blockage instead.
why: Hair binds with soap into a plug that slowly blocks the pipe. Catching it early stops the blockage forming.

title: Fat goes in the bin, not the sink
excerpt: Cooking fat sets like candle wax in the pipes. Here’s what to do with it instead.
steps: Never pour oil or fat down the sink, even with hot water.
Let it cool in an old jar or tin, then put it in the general waste bin.
Wipe greasy pans and plates with kitchen roll before you wash them.
why: Fat cools and hardens in the pipes, catches everything else and causes blocked sinks and smells.

title: Only flush the 3 Ps
excerpt: Toilets are built for three things. Everything else causes blockages.
steps: Only flush pee, poo and toilet paper.
Wipes, pads, tampons, cotton buds and kitchen roll go in the bin, even “flushable” wipes.
Keep a small bin with a lid in the bathroom.
why: Wipes and pads don’t break down. They tangle in the pipes and cause blockages that affect the whole house.

title: Test your smoke alarm every month
excerpt: A ten-second test once a month makes sure your smoke alarm will wake you if it needs to.
steps: Once a month, press and hold the test button until it beeps.
If it doesn’t beep, or it chirps every so often, report it straight away.
Never take the battery out, and never cover the alarm, even when cooking.
why: Smoke alarms save lives, but only if they work. A quick test is the only way to know.

title: Keep fire doors shut
excerpt: A closed fire door gives everyone in the house time to get out. A propped one gives none.
steps: Keep fire doors closed at all times, especially in shared areas.
Never prop or wedge them open.
Know your way out of the building.
If a fire door doesn’t close fully by itself, or a seal is damaged, report it straight away.
why: Fire doors hold back fire and toxic smoke, which is often more dangerous than the flames, giving you time to escape.

title: Power off? Check for a tripped switch
excerpt: Most power cuts in one room are a tripped switch you can reset in seconds.
steps: Find the fuse box (consumer unit).
Look for a switch pointing down.
Unplug anything that was on when the power went, then push the switch back up.
If it trips again, leave it off and report it. Never reset it if you smell burning.
why: A trip switch cuts the power when something is faulty, to keep you safe. Resetting once is fine; if it keeps tripping, an electrician needs to look.

title: Leave the washing machine open
excerpt: Leaving the door ajar after a wash stops that musty washing machine smell.
steps: Take washing out as soon as the cycle finishes.
Leave the door and detergent drawer open so the machine dries out.
Wipe the rubber door seal now and then and clear out anything caught in it.
why: A closed, damp drum and seal are perfect for mould, which makes the machine and your clothes smell.

title: Ice in the freezer? Defrost it
excerpt: Thick ice makes a freezer work harder and keep food less cold. Here’s how to defrost it safely.
steps: Move food into a cool bag, or plan it for a day the freezer is nearly empty.
Switch the freezer off and leave the door open.
Put towels down to catch the water.
Let the ice melt by itself. Never chip at it with a knife.
Dry inside, switch it back on, and wait until it’s cold before refilling.
why: Chipping at ice can puncture the cooling pipes and break the freezer.

title: Right bin, right day
excerpt: Bins done right keep the house clean, keep pests away and keep the council happy.
steps: Check your bin collection days in the Capital Rooms app.
Rinse and flatten recycling; food waste goes in its own caddy.
If a bin is full, take it out and put a new liner in. Don’t wait for someone else.
Put bins out the night before collection and bring them back in.
why: Overflowing or wrongly sorted bins attract pests and can mean the council won’t collect them.

title: Keep food sealed, keep pests away
excerpt: Mice only move in where there’s food. Sealed tubs and clean sides keep them out.
steps: Keep dry food in sealed tubs, not open packets.
Wipe the sides and sweep up crumbs after cooking.
Don’t leave dirty dishes or food out overnight.
If you see a mouse or droppings, report it straight away.
why: Pests follow food. Taking away easy food is the most effective way to stop them coming in.

title: Spotted a drip? Report it early
excerpt: A small drip is cheap to fix today. Left alone, it can bring a ceiling down.
steps: If you see a drip, a damp patch or water where it shouldn’t be, take a photo.
Report it in the Capital Rooms app straight away.
Put a bowl or towel underneath in the meantime.
If water is pouring, turn off the stopcock and report it as an emergency.
why: Leaks get worse quickly and can damage ceilings, floors and electrics. Reporting early means a small, quick fix.

title: Heading out? Lock up
excerpt: Most break-ins are through an unlocked door or window. Lock up every time you go out.
steps: Close and lock your windows before you go out.
Lock your bedroom door and make sure the front door is locked behind you.
Never leave keys under mats or in letterboxes.
If you lose a key, tell us straight away.
why: An unlocked door or open window is the easiest way in for a burglar, and it affects everyone in the house.
